page.title: Day 6 against Neave's manual
page.standfirst_html: Every flag the comparator raised for Day 6, adjudicated against I.Day.6.19Feb22.pdf — the extracted text for wording, and twenty-three page images for emphasis, layout and the things that were never transcribed at all. Day 6 is the noisiest day yet: 76 flagged sentences, but half of them trace to two causes that turn out to be harmless. What is left is not harmless. Decide each one; export the file; I make the edits and open the PR.

sections.title: Fix proposed
sections.note_html: Each one is a word-for-word difference from the source that I judge a transcription defect. Blue underline is what Neave wrote; struck red is what the site says instead. Two are severe enough to change what the reader understands: the photo caption on printed p7, which invents fifty words, and the dropped clause on printed p23, which leaves a sentence with no verb.

items.source_html: Reactive behaviour, managing by results [MBR].
items.site_html: Reactive behaviour, managing by results [ABBR].
items.proposal: Reactive behaviour, managing by results *[MBR]*.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image: Neave's editorial gloss is [MBR] — Management by Results, the abbreviation the rest of the paragraph then uses ("Manage by results: quality goes down"). ABBR is not an abbreviation of anything; it looks like a transcription placeholder that was never filled in.

items.flag: not flagged — inside a clean-matching sentence
items.source_html: As Dr [Myron] Tribus put it: while driving your automobile…
items.site_html: As Dr Myron Tribus put it: while driving your automobile…
items.proposal: As Dr *[Myron]* Tribus put it: while driving your automobile, keeping your eye on the rear-view mirror, what would happen?
items.evidence_html: Neave's convention throughout this material is that a square-bracketed italic run is his insertion into someone else's words — Day 6 uses it five more times ([fired or quit], [bag], [a cartoon character used in some of the videos], [the Government's Health Secretary], [see pages 23–24]). Here the brackets were dropped and the italic run slid one word left, so the site reads as if "Dr Myron" were a title Deming used. Deming said "Dr Tribus"; Neave supplied the first name.

items.source_html: So I found the Joiner Triangle to be absolutely ideal for my learning back in <mark class='src'>1986</mark>.
items.site_html: So I found the Joiner Triangle to be absolutely ideal for my learning back in <mark class='gone'>1988</mark>.
items.proposal: So I found the Joiner Triangle to be absolutely ideal for my learning back in 1986.
items.evidence_html: Read straight off the page image, last line of printed p2. This is the one class of defect similarity scoring cannot see — one digit inside a long sentence still scores 94%, which is why the reference-token rule exists (#738).

items.flag: not flagged — inside a clean-matching paragraph
items.source_html: …they are not short but at least they do not involve <mark class='src'>quite</mark> such deep thinking!
items.site_html: …they are not short but at least they do not involve such deep thinking!
items.proposal: Today's Activities are relatively straightforward compared with many others elsewhere in the course—they are not short but at least they do not involve quite such deep thinking!
items.evidence_html: "quite such" hedges the claim; "such" asserts it flatly. Verified in the extracted text and on the page image.

items.source_html: …score 5 if the organisation uses no kind of <mark class='src'>(judgmental)</mark> appraisal system… relatively informal and is less concerned with judging and <mark class='src'>scaring</mark> than with coaching and helping.
items.site_html: …score 5 if the organisation uses no kind of <mark class='gone'>judgmental</mark> appraisal system… relatively informal and is less concerned with judging and <mark class='gone'>scoring</mark> than with coaching and helping.
items.proposal: …uses no kind of (judgmental) appraisal system, 0 if there is a feared, *extremely* judgmental appraisal scheme… less concerned with judging and scaring than with coaching and helping.
items.evidence_html: Two changes on one line. scaring → scoring is the substantive one: Neave's pairing is judging and scaring against coaching and helping — fear against help, which is Point 8's whole argument. "scoring" makes it a sentence about marking. The parentheses around "(judgmental)" are Neave hedging his own word before he uses it unhedged in the next clause.

items.source_html: <mark class='src'>There</mark> they sat, all dressed alike, wearing maroon-coloured tee-shirts displaying the single word “GALLERY” in large letters.
items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>Then</mark> they sat, all dressed alike, wearing maroon-coloured tee-shirts displaying the single word "GALLERY" in large letters.
items.proposal: There they sat, all dressed alike, wearing maroon-coloured tee-shirts displaying the single word "GALLERY" in large letters.
items.evidence_html: "There they sat" is Neave pointing at the front row he has just described. "Then they sat" turns it into a sequence of events, and contradicts the previous sentence, which already has them seated.

items.source_html: Mack tells the story of Gallery Furniture for the first time at a Deming seminar on 12 July 1991, Washington DC. Also participating were three of his colleagues<mark class='src'>:</mark> (left to right) Mary Dunstan (Personnel Director), Don Ledford <mark class='src'>(Sales) and Mark Gervisch (Sales and Training). The session was chaired by Ed Baker (behind Mark)</mark> who was Bill Scherkenbach’s successor at the Ford Motor Company after Bill had moved on to assist General Motors.
items.site_html: Mack tells the story of Gallery Furniture for the first time at a Deming seminar on 12 July 1991, Washington DC. Also participating were three of his colleagues<mark class='gone'>,</mark> (left to right) Mary Dunstan (Personnel Director), Don Ledford <mark class='gone'>(Sales and Mark Gervich. Standing at right is Bill Scherkenbach (then Chairman of the British Deming Association and prior to that a statistician with the Nashua Corporation, then a quality consultant with the Ford Motor Company, and then Quality Director at General Motors. The person at far left, half-hidden by Mack)</mark> who was Bill Scherkenbach's successor at the Ford Motor Company after Bill had moved on to assist General Motors.
items.proposal: ![Mack tells the story of Gallery Furniture for the first time at a Deming seminar on 12 July 1991, Washington DC. Also participating were three of his colleagues: (left to right) Mary Dunstan (Personnel Director), Don Ledford (Sales) and Mark Gervisch (Sales and Training). The session was chaired by Ed Baker (behind Mark) who was Bill Scherkenbach's successor at the Ford Motor Company after Bill had moved on to assist General Motors.](/assets/images/day-06/mack-seminar-group.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .lightbox}
items.evidence_html: The worst defect on the day, and the report only reached it at 36% because so little of the caption survives. The site drops Don Ledford's role and Mark Gervisch's name and role, drops the fact that Ed Baker chaired the session, and splices in ~50 words about Bill Scherkenbach's career that appear nowhere in this caption — leaving "who was Bill Scherkenbach's successor" dangling with no antecedent and an unclosed parenthesis. Note the spelling: this caption says Gervisch, while printed p11 says Gervich. That inconsistency is Neave's own and the transcription should reproduce it, not normalise it.

items.chip: Parentheses turned into an exclamation mark
items.flag: not flagged — the sentence still matched its neighbour
items.source_html: …they are <mark class='src'>(as will be obvious to you)</mark> <mark class='src'>not technically</mark> of high quality but are at least honest copies of the genuine article!
items.site_html: …they are <mark class='gone'>as will be obvious to you!</mark> <mark class='gone'>not</mark> of high quality but are at least honest copies of the genuine article!
items.proposal: *This picture and that of Mack on the previous page are stills from the NTSC video of the event—and so, as on a few other occasions in this material (particularly during Day 2), they are (as will be obvious to you) not technically of high quality but are at least honest copies of the genuine article!*
items.evidence_html: The parenthetical aside became a mid-sentence exclamation mark, which makes the sentence ungrammatical, and "technically" was dropped — the word that limits the criticism to picture quality rather than to the material.

items.source_html: It was <mark class='src'>7.00 pm</mark> when we finished typing the ticket.
items.site_html: It was <mark class='gone'>7.00pm</mark> when we finished typing the ticket.
items.proposal: It was 7.00 pm when we finished typing the ticket.
items.evidence_html: Neave sets a thin space before "pm". This is the corpus's only N.NNpm, so there is no site convention it is following — see the deliberately-checked note in #734 about not calling a single instance a convention.

items.source_html: The thinking was that people worked harder for a carrot. <mark class='src'>But all that changed were the faces.</mark>
items.site_html: The thinking was that people worked harder for a carrot. <mark class='gone'>But all that changed when the faces were the faces.</mark>
items.proposal: There was a daily sales goal. And, at the high point of this madness, if the goal was reached then the 1st-placed salesperson for the day received a $500 cash bonus, the 2nd-placed got $300, and the 3rd-placed got $200. The thinking was that people worked harder for a carrot. But all that changed were the faces.
items.evidence_html: The site's sentence is not English. Mack's point — the incentives changed nothing about the system, only which individuals won it that week — is completely lost.

items.source_html: If they drove <mark class='src'>in in</mark> a big Mercedes, they’d get a lot of service. If they drove <mark class='src'>in in</mark> an old Ford Taurus, they wouldn’t get any.
items.site_html: If they drove <mark class='gone'>in</mark> a big Mercedes, they'd get a lot of service. If they drove <mark class='gone'>in</mark> an old Ford Taurus, they wouldn't get any.
items.proposal: …And they would prejudge every customer before they walked in the door based on the type of car they drove in on. If they drove in in a big Mercedes, they'd get a lot of service. If they drove in in an old Ford Taurus, they wouldn't get any.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image — both sentences read "drove in in". It is Mack's spoken idiom (drove in, in a Mercedes), matching "the type of car they drove in on" in the sentence before. Judgment call: this is the one finding where I would understand declining — it reads like a typo, and the site's version is smoother. But the pass is word-for-word, and it is what he wrote, twice.

items.source_html: <mark class='src'>Ranking</mark> and averages
items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>Rankings</mark> and averages
items.proposal: ### Ranking and averages {#sec-page10}
items.evidence_html: The section is about ranking as a management practice, not about a set of rankings — the paragraph beneath begins "The fear came from ranking". The short-content pass caught this because a four-word heading cannot support a similarity score.

items.source_html: Dr Deming calls this “tampering”—and, believe me, I did <mark class='src'>lots of it.</mark>
items.site_html: Dr Deming calls this "tampering"—and, believe me, I did <mark class='gone'>a lot of it!</mark>
items.proposal: …Dr Deming calls this "tampering"—and, believe me, I did lots of it.
items.evidence_html: Both the wording and the final stop differ. The page image shows a full stop, not an exclamation mark; pdftotext's trailing ! here is the footnote-font artifact that appears throughout this PDF.

items.source_html: <mark class='src'>Now 43%</mark> wasn’t bad, seeing the national furniture industry average was <mark class='src'>24%</mark>.
items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>Now, 43%</mark> wasn't bad, seeing the national furniture industry average was <mark class='gone'>33%</mark>.
items.proposal: …seemed to never get above 43%. Now 43% wasn't bad, seeing the national furniture industry average was 24%. But no matter how many extra incentives we offered…
items.evidence_html: The site understates how far ahead of the industry Gallery already was — 43% against 24% is nearly double; against 33% it is a modest lead. That materially weakens Mack's setup for why chasing a higher closing rate was tampering. The added comma after "Now" goes with it.

items.source_html: They were <mark class='src'>consistently</mark> going ahead of their friends in the “batting-order basis” in which customers were served.
items.site_html: They were <mark class='gone'>constantly</mark> going ahead of their friends in the "batting-order basis" in which customers were served.
items.proposal: They were consistently going ahead of their friends in the "batting-order basis" in which customers were served.
items.evidence_html: "consistently" says the queue-jumping was systematic — the point of the sentence, since the top ten had won the right to it for a whole month. "constantly" says only that it happened often.

items.source_html: Never! I had grown up in a world of competition: I win, you lose—beat the other guy. I had grown up in a world of incentives.
items.site_html: Never! I had <mark class='gone'>never</mark> grown up in a world of competition: I win, you lose—beat the other guy. I had grown up in a world of incentives.
items.proposal: …But: eliminate merit pay, incentive pay, and commissions? Never! I had grown up in a world of competition: I win, you lose—beat the other guy. I had grown up in a world of incentives. I had grown up in a world of building superstar mentality.
items.evidence_html: A spurious "never" reverses the sentence and breaks the rhetorical triple that follows it — Mack says "I had grown up in a world of…" three times running, and the site's version denies the first of the three. The "Never!" that precedes it is his answer to the previous question, not part of this clause.

items.source_html: Someone asked me, at one of the Deming <mark class='src'>downlinks</mark>, if I would go back to commission if our sales were to slide.
items.site_html: Someone asked me, at one of the Deming <mark class='gone'>downfalls</mark>, if I would go back to commission if our sales were to slide.
items.proposal: Someone asked me, at one of the Deming downlinks, if I would go back to commission if our sales were to slide.
items.evidence_html: A "Deming downlink" was a satellite broadcast of a Deming seminar to remote sites — a real thing, and where the question was put to Mack. "downfalls" is not a place a question can be asked at, and reads as a comment on Deming.

items.flag: not flagged — below the reference rule
items.source_html: I learned to compete at the University of Texas in 1969<mark class='src'>–</mark>70.
items.site_html: I learned to compete at the University of Texas in 1969<mark class='gone'>-</mark>70.
items.proposal: I learned to compete at the University of Texas in 1969–70.
items.evidence_html: Neave sets an en dash in the year span, as the site already does elsewhere on this day (pages 62--63[72--73] at 04-more-true-stories.qmd:21, pages 23--24). This is the one place on Day 6 that uses a plain hyphen for a span.

items.source_html: Here is a comparison of Gallery <mark class='src'>before</mark> we eliminated commissions with how management has totally changed their view today:
items.site_html: Here is a comparison of Gallery <mark class='gone'>before and after</mark> we eliminated commissions with how management has totally changed their view today:
items.proposal: In order for transformation to occur, the biggest change has to take place in management's thinking. Here is a comparison of Gallery before we eliminated commissions with how management has totally changed their view today:
items.evidence_html: "before and after we eliminated commissions" makes the second half of the sentence redundant and mis-parses the comparison: Neave's sentence contrasts Gallery before with management's view today. Two words added that are not in the source.

items.source_html: As recommended on Day 5 page 28, I hope you have been able to supply yourself with an enlarged copy of this table: you will find it very useful to be able to compare the two situations side-by-side, but at the current size you have little space in which to insert your comments, etc. You will also find it particularly convenient to be able to refer to this table directly (without having to keep turning back) while completing this Major Activity—see page 20.
items.site_html: (the paragraph does not appear on the site at all)
items.proposal:
Both to save space, and for ease of comparison, I am providing you with the single table below on which you can write your thoughts on both the "Before" and "After" exercises. Leave the central yellow column blank for now.

As recommended on [Day 5 page 28](../day-05/03-the-deadly-diseases.qmd#sec-page28), I hope you have been able to supply yourself with an enlarged copy of this table: you will find it very useful to be able to compare the two situations side-by-side, but at the current size you have little space in which to insert your comments, etc.
items.evidence_html: The only whole paragraph of Neave's prose absent from Day 6. Its second half is print-specific ("without having to keep turning back", "see page 20") and does not survive the web layout — but its first half is live advice that the next paragraph on the site already depends on, referring back to "that 'out-of-hours' note" with nothing on the page having introduced it. Judgment call: my proposal restores the first sentence and drops the turning-back clause; declining leaves the forward reference dangling, so if you'd rather have all of it or none of it, say which.

items.source_html: You could then start at the top of the table on the next page with Point 1 and work through each of the 19 rows issue by issue, to end with Deadly Disease 5.
items.site_html: You could then start at the top of the table with Point 1 and work through each of the 19 rows issue by issue, to end with Deadly Disease 5.
items.proposal: You *could* then start at the top of [the table on page 19](#sec-page19) with Point 1 and work through each of the 19 rows issue by issue, to end with Deadly Disease 5.
items.evidence_html: "on the next page" is print-specific, but the site drops the pointer rather than re-aiming it, leaving "the table" ambiguous in a paragraph that has just discussed Mack's account. The #sec-page19 anchor already exists eight lines below (03-activity-6b.qmd:27), so the enriched-link form from #610 resolves. Italic could is a separate finding in the emphasis group.

items.flag: not flagged — inside a clean-matching paragraph
items.source_html: <mark class='src'>Finally for the time being</mark>, work through the table one more time…
items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>Finally, for the time being,</mark> work through the table one more time…
items.proposal: Finally for the time being, work through the table one more time, now considering the comments you have made on both the "Pre-Deming" and "Post-Deming" sides of the table.
items.evidence_html: Neave punctuates "Finally for the time being" as one unit; the site's extra comma splits it into two hedges in a row. Small, but it is a difference from the source and nothing else records that it was looked at.

items.flag: not flagged — inside a clean-matching paragraph
items.source_html: He agreed that I needed the operation; but, in view of factors such as my weight, blood pressure, and home circumstances…
items.site_html: He agreed that I needed the operation<mark class='gone'>,</mark> but, in view of factors such as my weight, blood pressure, and home circumstances…
items.proposal: He agreed that I needed the operation; *but*, in view of factors such as my weight, blood pressure, and home circumstances, I was outside the criteria required to have the operation performed as a day-patient: I would need to stay in hospital overnight.
items.evidence_html: The semicolon marks the pivot of the anecdote — agreement, then the obstruction. Three commas in a row flattens it. The italic but is the same pivot and is listed in the emphasis group; the proposal carries both.

items.chip: Dropped clause makes the sentence meaningless
items.source_html: According to this performance indicator, Grades C and above counted toward the school’s “score”, Grades D and below did not. The Grade C club comprised those pupils who were considered likely to produce passes at either grade C or grade D.
items.site_html: According to this performance indicator, Grades D and below did not. The Grade C club comprised those pupils who were considered likely to produce passes at either <mark class='gone'>Grade C</mark> or grade D.
items.proposal: …In Britain, schools had for some considerable time been ranked ("league-tabled") according to the proportion of passes recorded in national examinations at grades C and above. According to this performance indicator, Grades C and above counted toward the school's "score", Grades D and below did not. The Grade C club comprised those pupils who were considered likely to produce passes at *either* grade C *or* grade D.
items.evidence_html: "According to this performance indicator, Grades D and below did not" — did not what? The clause the verb belongs to was dropped, and with it the entire mechanism the story is about: the grade boundary that made D-grade pupils worthless to the league table. Neave also writes lower-case "grade C" in the next sentence, where the site capitalises it.

items.source_html: …protecting ministers from political criticism over Labour’s stewardship of the <mark class='src'>Service</mark>.
items.site_html: …protecting ministers from political criticism over Labour's stewardship of the <mark class='gone'>NHS</mark>.
items.proposal: He will paint a picture of the NHS gripped by a "culture of fear" as managers became fixated on meeting targets and protecting ministers from political criticism over Labour's stewardship of the Service.
items.evidence_html: This is quoted matter — an extract from The Telegraph reproduced with the Telegraph Media Group's approval (footnote a, printed p27). The paper wrote "the Service", varying from "the NHS" earlier in the same sentence; the site repeats "NHS" twice. Fidelity matters more than usual in a passage carried under a rights approval.

items.source_html: And yet the evidence we <mark class='src'>took</mark> was that rape, for example, might be as much as 25% under-recorded by the Metropolitan Police.
items.site_html: And yet the evidence we <mark class='gone'>got</mark> was that rape, for example, might be as much as 25% under-recorded by the Metropolitan Police.
items.proposal: And yet the evidence we took was that rape, for example, might be as much as 25% under-recorded by the Metropolitan Police.
items.evidence_html: "the evidence we took" is select-committee usage — a committee takes evidence — and Jenkin is Chairman of the Public Administration Committee, speaking about his own enquiry. Also quoted matter, carried under the BBC's approval (footnote b).

items.source_html: There is a habit <mark class='src'>engrained</mark> by the target culture which both parties in various places in Government have been tempted to use.
items.site_html: There is a habit <mark class='gone'>engendered</mark> by the target culture which both parties in various places in Government have been tempted to use.
items.proposal: There is a habit engrained by the target culture which both parties in various places in Government have been tempted to use.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image. "engendered" is the more idiomatic word and is very likely why it slipped in, but Neave's transcript of the broadcast says "engrained", and this is quoted matter carried under the BBC's approval.

items.flag: not flagged — inside a clean-matching paragraph
items.source_html: …from the Francis enquiry into Mid-Staffordshire [see pages 23–24], that the target culture drove people to be secretive…
items.site_html: …from the Francis enquiry into Mid-Staffordshire (see pages 23--24), that the target culture drove people to be secretive…
items.proposal: We know, for example, from the Francis enquiry into Mid-Staffordshire *[see [pages 23--24](#sec-page23)]*, that the target culture drove people to be secretive and to hide the truth and not deal with what was going on.
items.evidence_html: Square brackets, not parentheses — this is Neave inserting a pointer into Jenkin's spoken words, and the bracket is what marks it as not-Jenkin. Same convention as D6-02. The site's parentheses read as if the MP said it.

sections.title: Emphasis, found only in the page images
sections.note_html: pdftotext discards every italic and bold, so no automated flag in this epic can see any of these — all fifteen came from reading the source pages directly. Day 6 leans on italics harder than Day 5 did: Neave builds three separate arguments out of italicised contrasts (theory/practice, unique/universal, leap/hop), and the site sets all of them in roman.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html:
…we are learning about Dr Deming’s theory of management. But… the purpose of that theory is to guide better practice… into practice—distinctly better practice!

…they are necessarily unique, whereas the Deming theory is universal… will necessitate different ways of applying the theory… not with the intention of copying it but of learning from it.
items.site_html: …all eight set in roman on the site; only "learning from it" is italic, and its italic run wrongly swallows the "it".
items.proposal:
…learning about Dr Deming's *theory* of management. … the purpose of that *theory* is to guide better *practice*. … distinctly *better* practice!

…necessarily *unique*, whereas the Deming theory is *universal*. … will necessitate *different* ways of *applying* the theory. … not with the intention of *copying* it but of *learning from* it.
items.evidence_html: Neave's whole argument on printed p1 is carried by these italic contrasts — theory against practice, unique against universal, copying against learning from. Set in roman they read as ordinary prose and the contrast disappears. pdftotext discards every italic, so no automated flag in this epic can see any of it.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: …recognising what is definitely not based on Dr Deming's theory! … You may find it difficult to believe a few of them, but they are all true!
items.site_html: …recognising what is definitely not based on Dr Deming's theory! … but they are all true!
items.proposal: …already very capable of recognising what is definitely *not* based on Dr Deming's theory! … You may find it difficult to believe a few of them, but they *are* all true!
items.evidence_html: Both are stress marks on a single word, which is exactly the kind of emphasis that carries the sentence's tone and exactly the kind pdftotext throws away.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: 0 if there is a feared, extremely judgmental appraisal scheme used throughout the organisation…
items.site_html: 0 if there is a feared, extremely judgmental appraisal scheme used throughout the organisation…
items.proposal: …0 if there is a feared, *extremely* judgmental appraisal scheme used throughout the organisation…
items.evidence_html: The italic is what separates the 0 end of the scale from the "(judgmental)" hedge four words earlier — same sentence, and the parentheses there are D6-05. Both come from the same page image.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: …we decided our unique selling feature at Gallery Furniture would be immediate delivery.
items.site_html: …we decided our unique selling feature at Gallery Furniture would be immediate delivery.
items.proposal: So, from Day 1, we decided our unique selling feature at Gallery Furniture would be *immediate delivery*.
items.evidence_html: The one italic run on printed p7, marking the phrase Mack then repeats twice more as the store's defining promise.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: …he had his lunch in a paper sack [bag], and left it in the back of the break-room.
items.site_html: …he had his lunch in a paper sack [bag], and left it in the back of the break-room.
items.proposal: …and he had his lunch in a paper sack *[bag],* and left it in the back of the break-room.
items.evidence_html: The brackets survived but the italics did not, so nothing distinguishes Neave's gloss on Mack's Americanism from Mack's own words. Same convention as D6-02 and D6-28; here it is only the italics that are missing.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: Salary vs commission (heading) · Carl and I discussed salary pay vs commission · what Team Handbook’s author Peter Scholtes describes · we took not a leap but a hop of faith
items.site_html: Salary vs commission · salary pay vs commission · what Team Handbook's author · we took not a leap but a hop of faith
items.evidence_html: Four on one page. The leap/hop pair is the important one — the site italicises only "hop", so the contrast the section title is built on ("The hop of faith", then "The leap of faith") lands on one side only. "Team Handbook's" is the boundary case: the possessive s belongs outside the italic, since it is not part of the book's title.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: But at least the problems would be new. And I have to admit that I was sick and tired of the same old problems… And things had to change!
items.site_html: But at least the problems would be new. … sick and tired of the same old problems… And things had to change!
items.proposal: And Dr Baker told me that any change would bring with it a whole new set of problems. But at least the problems would be *new*. And I have to admit that I was sick and tired of the same *old* problems, like battles over commission when more than one salesperson helped a customer, making payroll a real nightmare. New problems would be a welcome change. And things *had* to change!
items.evidence_html: The new/old pair is Dr Baker's joke and the paragraph's whole point; "had" is the beat the section ends on.

items.chip: Quote styled differently from its twin
items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: “Will you ever learn?” — indented, blue, regular weight, exactly as “I’m doing this because I have a responsibility to make a difference.” is set on printed p16.
items.site_html: > "Will you ever learn?" — a bold-italic blockquote, where the file's other Deming quotation uses <span class="deming_quote">.
items.proposal: "Will you ever learn?"
items.evidence_html: Neave sets Deming's own words in blue on both pages, and the site already has a class for exactly that — deming_quote, used in 44 files across all twelve days, including once in this very file at line 265 for the other blue quotation. Bold-italic adds emphasis the source does not have and makes the two sister quotes look like different kinds of thing.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: They now see the business as a system… Now we view the organisation as a system: How is the system doing?
items.site_html: They now see the business as a system… How is the system doing?
items.proposal:
They now see the business as a *system*, and the phrase "That's not my job" has completely disappeared.

Now we view the organisation as a system: How is the *system* doing?
items.evidence_html: Both italics land on the same word, and it is the word Day 9 onward is entirely about. Without them the two sentences read as description rather than as the arrival of a concept.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: No! Absolutely not! The biggest benefits of salary vs commission are unknown and unknowable.
items.site_html: No! Absolutely not! The biggest benefits of salary vs commission are unknown and unknowable.
items.proposal: Someone asked me, at one of the Deming downlinks, if I would go back to commission if our sales were to slide. *No! Absolutely not!* The biggest benefits of salary *vs* commission are unknown and unknowable.
items.evidence_html: The italic "No! Absolutely not!" is the loudest moment in Mack's account and the section heading ("No going back") depends on it. Same line as D6-17; the proposal there carries the wording fix, this one the italics.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: You could then start at the top of the table… Then, after completing that, now comes the time when I would advise you to start at the top of the table…
items.site_html: You could then start at the top of the table… now comes the time when I would advise you…
items.proposal:
You *could* then start at the top of the table… 

Then, after completing that, now comes the time when I *would* advise you to start at the top of the table and work through it, issue by issue.
items.evidence_html: The pair is the instruction: could (but don't) in the first paragraph, would (now do) in the third. Set in roman, the two paragraphs appear to give the same advice twice and contradict each other.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: But: there was also much evidence that (a) the number of people awaiting relatively serious operations increased… He agreed that I needed the operation; but, in view of factors…
items.site_html: But: there was also much evidence that (a) … operations increased… He agreed that I needed the operation, but, in view of factors…
items.proposal:
And indeed, that number did decrease, admittedly by a rather tiny fraction. *But*: there was also much evidence that (a) the number of people awaiting relatively serious operations *increased*, and (b)…

…He agreed that I needed the operation; *but*, in view of factors such as my weight…
items.evidence_html: Both italic Buts are the hinge of their paragraph — the target was met and the thing the target existed to fix got worse. The second shares its line with D6-23's semicolon; the proposal there carries both.

items.flag: not flagged — invisible to the comparator
items.source_html: Ability to simultaneously meet the quota and do a respectable job for the customers was largely a matter of luck. · …considered likely to produce passes at either grade C or grade D.
items.site_html: Ability to simultaneously meet the quota and do a respectable job… · …passes at either Grade C or grade D.
items.proposal:
Ability to simultaneously meet the quota *and* do a respectable job for the customers was largely a matter of luck.

…considered likely to produce passes at *either* grade C *or* grade D.
items.evidence_html: The italic and is the whole gas-engineer story in one word: not quota, not good job — both at once. The either/or pair marks the boundary the Grade C club was built around; its line also carries D6-24's dropped clause.

items.site_html: The report, which will go first to Mr Hunt [the Government's Health Secretary] and is set to be published days later…

items.evidence_html: Third instance of the same convention on this day (D6-02, E-05, D6-28). Here the brackets survived and only the italics were lost — inside quoted Telegraph matter, so the italics are what mark the gloss as Neave's rather than the paper's.

sections.title: Confirmed non-defect
sections.note_html: Checked and cleared. Each is a comparator artifact or a documented site-wide convention, not something the site gets wrong — and between them they account for roughly two-thirds of Day 6's raw flag count. Accepting means the finding is closed with that reason recorded; decline if you want a second look.

items.source_html: Cover page: “I / DAY 6: GALLERY FURNITURE and OTHER TRUE STORIES”. Contents page: the itinerary, the section listing with printed page numbers, the day’s clock range “(9.00am – 12.45pm; 1.45pm – 3.30pm)”, and “(Some detailed timing guidance is provided during this Major Activity.)”
items.site_html: DAY 6: GALLERY FURNITURE AND OTHER TRUE STORIES — the running title from printed p1, with no binder letter, no clock range, and no reproduced contents page.
items.evidence_html: Four flags, one cause. The site's H1 matches the running title on printed p1 exactly; the flags compare it against the binder cover and the contents page. No day in the corpus carries the clock range in its heading (checked across all twelve ## DAY N: headings), and no day reproduces its contents page — the site's own navigation replaces it. Nothing to fix.

items.flag: Gap — yellow banners; also the “[WB 100]” pointer on printed p16
items.source_html: “Activity 6–a (pages 4–5) is also on Workbook pages 98–99.” · “Major Activity 6–b (pages 18–21) is also on Workbook pages 100–103.” · “(Now please move on to page 18 [WB 100] …)”
items.site_html: None of the three appear on the site.
items.evidence_html: Workbook cross-references were removed corpus-wide and the decision is already on the record — docs/deviations/2026-04-21-remove-inline-see-workbook-p-n-page-reference-call-outs.md, …-rewrite-or-remove-workbook-references-from-prose-and-front-m.md and …2026-04-23-strip-inline-wb-nnn-cross-reference-suffixes.md. Confirmed against the corpus: zero matches for WB or "Workbook page" anywhere under content/, so this is a real convention and not a single-instance one.

items.chip: pdftotext read a table as prose
items.source_html: The 14 Points / Deadly Diseases scoring grids on printed pp5, 19 and 21, and the BEFORE / AFTER comparison on printed p15 — read by pdftotext as run-together prose (“Individual events, firefighting, kicking butt, View company as a whole—not focus on and taking names individual events”).
items.site_html: All three ship as cropped PNGs — scoring-table.png and before-after-table.png — with the Before/After table additionally carrying a full row-by-row text description in a <details> block.
items.evidence_html: Roughly half of Day 6's flag count, from one cause. I checked the Before/After description against the page image row by row and all twelve cells are accurate, including the [Return On Investment] gloss. The chain-effect ladder on printed p15 (Altered 31, eight flags) is likewise present and correctly indented at 02-gallery-furniture.qmd:233–249; the flags are the arrows being scored against LaTeX \rightarrow markup.

items.source_html: 1%'14' · 5'N4' · O'P4 · 5'54$ — and whole runs such as 5'N4' T0-B$>="1$#-.K0)$9"#4+(G
items.site_html: Dr D: · P O: · B J: · P P: — and the interviewer's questions transcribed in full.
items.evidence_html: Neave sets the interviewers' turns in a font pdftotext cannot decode, so every question in both transcripts comes back as cipher. That single cause produces three of the five reference mismatches (the “1, 14” and “1, 1, 2, 34” tokens are the garbled labels, not page numbers) and nine of the eleven unsourced flags (the site's real text has nothing in the extracted PDF to match against). Verified against the page images for printed pp1–2, 25 and 26: the site's labels and question text are correct.

items.source_html: Section headings that carry their citation on the same line (“7. Stafford Hospital (extracted from The Telegraph…)”, “2. Answering the telephone (from Out of the Crisis pages 62–63[72–73])”); the two-deck Stafford headline; the “Is it: / To make 25 calls per hour? / or / To give callers courteous satisfaction” ladder; the Approvals page.
items.site_html: Each split into its natural web parts — heading, then citation line; headline, then standfirst; the question ladder as separate lines; the approvals as footnotes [^a] and [^b].
items.evidence_html: Eight flags, all of them the comparator scoring one PDF block against a fragment of the site's equivalent. Every piece is present: I checked the telephone ladder against printed p22 (both alternatives and the italic or are there, at 04-more-true-stories.qmd:25–29) and both footnotes against printed p27 word for word.

items.source_html: (no PDF counterpart — the table is an image in the source)
items.site_html: "A two-column Before / After table contrasting Gallery Furniture's old and new management mindset, row by row…" and the Activity 6-b prompt "Score Gallery Furniture in its 'pre-Deming' state…"
items.evidence_html: Exactly what the unsourced section says it expects: figure descriptions and activity prompts that only ever existed on the site. The description is the accessible text alternative for before-after-table.png; the prompt is the label on a workbook textarea. Both correct, neither transcribed from anything.

items.flag: part of the QMD-only reference tokens in the mismatch section
items.source_html: …you might like to remind yourself about “fudging figures” (Day 5 page 10)! — the phrase is the link in the source; the page number is plain.
items.site_html: …remind yourself about "fudging figures" (Day 5 page 10)! — the page number is the link.
items.evidence_html: #610's house style, decided by the #582 spike: the page reference carries the link and the prose is not rewritten. Day 6 uses it in six places. Moving the anchor from the phrase to the page number is what generates the “QMD only” reference tokens the mismatch section warns about.
items.decision_note: Ok, but "fudging figures" should be blue text as it is in the original (i.e. a Deming quote)
items.outcome: The link-text convention stands: the page number keeps the anchor and the prose is not rewritten. Lee's point is separate and correct — Neave sets “fudging figures” in blue on printed p3, so the phrase is now wrapped in <span class="deming_quote">, the class the corpus already uses for Neave's blue Deming-quote runs. Verified against the page image. Applied in #775.

sections.title: Real, but not Day 6's to fix
sections.note_html: A genuine difference from the source that a per-day pass is the wrong instrument for.

items.flag: not flagged — no automated check covers figures
items.source_html: Printed p12 carries a photograph beside the Bart Simpson paragraph: a still of Mack in front of a hand-drawn Bart saying “Radical Move Dude!”, the drawing he is quoting.
items.site_html: The text is present; the photograph is not. assets/images/day-06/ holds four images — Mack, the seminar group, the Before/After table and the scoring table — and no fifth.
items.evidence_html: A genuine difference from the source, and the crop itself would take five minutes. But no per-day pass has a rule for deciding which source figures must ship — that is #725's spike ("what would figure/PNG fidelity validation even look like?"), which is open and explicitly scoped as research. Deciding this one photo here sets a precedent for eleven other days by accident. My recommendation is to note it against #725 so the sweep catches it with everything else; if you'd rather just have the picture, say so and I'll crop it into this PR.
items.outcome: Raised against #725 rather than cropped here, so the figure-fidelity rule is set once for all twelve days instead of by precedent from one photo.
